title: Practical dissipationless conductors and windings for bulk power systems

concept.text: The innovation is a manufacturable superconducting conductor, cable or winding that carries utility-scale current in relevant magnetic fields, under practical operating conditions, with competitive whole-system cost and reliability. Superconducting conductors and applications already exist. The missing advance is their broader economical deployment in bulk power systems, where eliminating ordinary conductor resistance would produce a dependable advantage over conventional equipment.

Two routes could satisfy this goal: materials that superconduct at warmer temperatures while carrying useful currents in field, or sufficiently economical and reliable systems built around cryogenic superconductors. Room-temperature, ambient-pressure operation would be especially valuable because it could remove the need to refrigerate the conductor. It is not a prerequisite for a successful power-system application, and a high laboratory transition temperature alone would not establish practical cable or winding performance.

significance.text: For a specified resistance, ordinary conductor heating increases as I²R. Removing that resistive heating from superconducting portions of cables and windings could substantially change their thermal limits and design choices. Compact, high-capacity transmission is a concrete opportunity: the announced Munich SuperLink design aims to carry 500 MW through a narrow urban corridor. Smaller or more efficient generators and motors are also plausible, but their benefits depend on the complete machine design, including the magnetic circuit, structural support and cooling equipment.

Engineering synthesis: zero conductor resistance would not make an entire alternating-current power system lossless or remove all reasons to use high voltage. Alternating-current losses, joints, auxiliaries, refrigeration, insulation, electromagnetic behavior, mechanical forces and fault protection would still constrain performance. Room-temperature operation could remove conductor refrigeration within the material's operating envelope; it would not eliminate these other losses and constraints. The revolutionary outcome would be a favorable complete system, rather than a resistance measurement considered alone.

The benefits would also have boundaries outside power delivery. Superconducting fusion magnets already exist; the supplied perspective identifies their use in ITER. Better conductors could improve such magnets, but practical fusion energy would remain a separate challenge. Neither lossless electronics nor a combined hydrogen-and-electricity pipeline follows automatically from a better power conductor. These are possible downstream connections requiring their own system demonstrations.

Engineering synthesis: zero resistance alone would not establish feasible seasonal magnetic energy storage. A storage system must also contain magnetic forces and meet requirements for capacity, cost, losses, safety and duration. The supplied research invokes a virial-theorem structural limit, but the cited paper was not retained for inspection in the review, so its specific comparison with existing magnet designs remains unverified here.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability combines materials discovery, industrial manufacture and system integration. A useful material must sustain adequate current in the magnetic fields and temperatures encountered in service, rather than merely exhibit a superconducting transition. The March 2026 perspective identifies prediction and synthesis as continuing obstacles: many predicted materials cannot yet be synthesized experimentally, and improved materials must also scale to industrial production. Its authors state that no known fundamental physical law rules out room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure; that position does not establish that an appropriate practical material exists or can be manufactured.

Engineering synthesis: translating a material into a power product requires consistent performance over useful lengths, workable connections and terminations, compatible insulation, and tolerance of electromagnetic forces and thermal cycling. A winding or cable also needs protection when superconductivity is locally lost, with acceptable recovery and replacement procedures. These are concrete qualification questions. The supplied evidence does not establish a general brittleness limit for superconducting tapes, quantified quench endurance, or decades-long service performance across the conductor family.

Economic integration is equally important. Refrigeration, cryostats, auxiliaries, maintenance and protection must fit the application's duty and cost limits. The earlier research cites a cable review for comparative costs, but that document was not captured in the supplied evidence. It therefore does not establish a general cost disadvantage relative to copper and aluminum. The unresolved goal is demonstrated competitive economics for specified applications, rather than proof that every existing superconducting installation is uneconomic.

current_state.text: On 9 March 2026, Deng and colleagues reported an ambient-pressure superconducting transition temperature of 151 K, approximately −122 °C, in pressure-quenched HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ. Their abstract describes this as a record following an ambient-pressure plateau unchanged since 1993. The figure captions available to the review identify the transition metric as onset and describe diamond-anvil-cell experiments. This is a reported laboratory materials result; it does not establish engineering current density in field, cable performance or utility service. The supplied review had the PubMed abstract and captions, rather than the full experimental paper, and did not inspect the plotted curves or images.

A UC Davis account dated 16 March 2026 reports that the enhanced superconducting state persisted for up to two weeks after rapid pressure removal, with the transition temperature up to 18 degrees higher. The PubMed abstract does not state that retention time, so the lifetime remains attributed to the university account rather than independently assessed primary measurements. The news account also mislabels its Fahrenheit conversion of 151 K; approximately −122 °C is the correct Celsius conversion.

On 15 April 2026, Stadtwerke München and NKT announced a letter of intent for SuperLink after what their release describes as successful operation of a Munich test system. The proposed commercial circuit would extend up to 15 km, carry 500 MW at 110 kV, and use liquid-nitrogen cooling to about −200 °C. These are announced specifications. The release says electrical losses would be almost completely avoided, but provides no whole-system life-cycle comparison. It also states that negotiations toward a binding contract were continuing; the announcement does not establish construction or commercial service.

The earlier research attributes several findings to a cable roadmap published on 2 February 2026: technically successful field tests, a few permanent installations generally around one kilometer and up to 154 kV alternating current, a technology-concept classification for high-voltage long-distance cables, higher cable-system costs associated with cooling and cryostats, and coated-conductor prices around €80–100 per kiloampere-meter at 77 K in self-field. No text of that review was retained in the supplied evidence, so these installation, readiness and cost details remain unverified here. The quoted conductor-price operating conditions would matter to interpretation even if the figure were confirmed.

The earlier research also describes EcoSwing as a field-tested 3.6 MW superconducting wind generator, citing a paper dated 25 October 2019, and reports a possible 40 percent weight reduction and more than 650 hours of grid generation. The supplied review had no retained artifact for that paper, so those numerical claims could not be checked. They remain reported pilot-scale results, not established evidence of a commercial product line or of competitive lifetime cost and reliability.

These sources describe dated achievements and proposals rather than a verified worldwide survey as of 1 November 2026. The supplied review contains no completed freshness search establishing whether the laboratory record, SuperLink contract status or commercialization picture subsequently changed. The March 2026 programmatic perspective was available to that review in full, correcting the earlier research's abstract-only access note. The experimental paper remained partially accessible. An unrelated UC Davis organization chart and a truncated SWM annual report do not resolve the substantive evidence gaps.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an official threshold: a multi-kilometer transmission-class circuit carrying hundreds of megawatts in ordinary utility service, with published life-cycle cost and forced-outage performance better than a conventional circuit of comparable rating and duty. The comparison should state its observation period, utilization, environmental conditions and accounting assumptions, and include cooling, auxiliaries, maintenance, protection and replacement. An urban corridor advantage should be distinguished from an advantage applicable to other routes.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-kilometer utility circuit beats conventional life-cycle cost and forced-outage performance

completion_criteria.text: An alternative proposed demonstration is a commercial generator whose superconducting winding demonstrably makes the complete machine smaller or less lossy than a comparable copper-wound machine, while maintaining acceptable total cost and reliability. Its comparison should include refrigeration and auxiliary equipment, installation requirements, maintenance and the operating duty. A successful pilot or a projected weight saving would be useful progress but would not by itself establish this commercial capability.
completion_criteria.label: Smaller or less lossy commercial generator maintains acceptable cost and reliability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed materials and reproducibility requirements: characterize transition temperature alongside engineering current density in relevant magnetic fields, operating margins, stability, mechanical behavior, joints and protection. Replicate material performance across independently produced batches and useful conductor lengths, and reproduce system results in independently assessable installations. A room-temperature, ambient-pressure wire could satisfy the materials route if it passed the applicable service demonstration; a laboratory onset-temperature record alone could not.
completion_criteria.label: Material performance replicates across batches and lengths; system results reproduce independently

completion_criteria.text: The demonstrated operating envelope should explicitly bound temperature, pressure, magnetic field, current, length, alternating- or direct-current duty, environmental exposure and maintenance needs. Finite tests would establish breadth within that envelope, not universal superiority. Continental gigawatt networks would remain a later deployment objective requiring further evidence on distance, protection, construction, reliability and economics, even after a successful local circuit.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated operating envelope explicitly bounds service conditions and maintenance needs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PWR-02, Solid-state conversion of heat to utility electricity, concerns converting thermal energy into electricity. PWR-01 concerns carrying current and constructing windings after or during electrical generation. Better conductors could reduce some electrical losses in a conversion installation, but they would not establish the heat-to-electricity conversion mechanism or its efficiency. The entries address distinct missing capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: PWR-03, Utility-scale electromagnetic delivery of power without a conductor, shares the objective of delivering substantial electrical power. PWR-01 depends on a physical conductor; PWR-03 seeks a delivery path without one. A superconducting component might assist equipment at either end of such a system, but it would not demonstrate efficient, practical power transfer across the intervening space.

Roster-based synthesis: PWR-04, Site-independent storage from multi-day weather through seasonal imbalance, addresses shifting energy through time. PWR-01 addresses conductors and windings. Superconducting magnetic storage is a possible overlap, but persistent current alone does not establish the capacity, structural feasibility, duration or economics needed for seasonal storage. The storage entry remains separate.

Roster-based synthesis: PWR-05, An interconnection that no longer depends on synchronous machines, concerns grid operation, stability and coordination. PWR-01 could change cables and machines within an interconnection, but it does not by itself supply the controls and electrical behavior required to operate without dependence on synchronous machines. Conversely, that grid architecture need not require superconducting conductors.

Additional conceptual synthesis: warmer superconductivity is a materials route within PWR-01, while continental gigawatt cables are an extension of its deployment scale. The earlier research's historical reference to hundreds-of-kilometers cables lacks inspectable support in this packet. Fault-current limiting is a distinct protection application: the earlier description of resistive limiters using the same tape family remains unverified here, and such a device should not be treated as evidence that economical dissipationless bulk-power delivery has been achieved.

unresolved_issues: Independent reproducibility, engineering current capacity in field, scalable manufacture and primary lifetime measurements for the reported pressure-quenched 151 K state remain unestablished by the supplied evidence.
The cable roadmap's installation survey, readiness classification, comparative costs and €80–100 per kiloampere-meter conductor-price estimate require inspectable source text.
EcoSwing's reported 3.6 MW rating, possible 40 percent weight reduction and more than 650 grid-generation hours require inspectable supporting text and clearer comparison boundaries.
The supplied material does not establish SuperLink's contract, construction or service status after 15 April 2026, or provide a complete life-cycle comparison.
General tape brittleness, comparative conductor expense, quench endurance and decades-long reliability were not established across the relevant conductor families.
The specific virial-theorem comparison with existing magnet structures, historical long-distance cable goal and tape-family details for resistive fault-current limiters remain unverified.
No completed freshness search establishes the worldwide state on 1 November 2026.
The proposed service tests have no fixed observation duration or accepted economic and reliability thresholds; those would need to be specified for each demonstration.

brief.title: Practical power cables and coils without resistance
possible: Cities could carry more electricity through narrow underground routes. Utilities could use superconductors, materials that carry current without electrical resistance, in affordable, reliable cables and generator coils. These coils are windings of wire that create magnetic fields.

Success could come from better materials or from making deeply cooled equipment economical and dependable. A material that worked at room temperature and ordinary pressure could remove the need to cool the conductor.
why: Removing resistance would reduce conductor heating and give power companies more freedom to design compact equipment. Generators could become smaller or waste less energy, while cities could increase transmission capacity where space is scarce.

Stadtwerke München and NKT reported a successful cable test. EcoSwing also reached generator field testing. Neither demonstration establishes the full combination of cost, reliability and performance needed for broader utility use.
missing: Long conductors must consistently carry useful currents in service magnetic fields and withstand mechanical stress and repeated cooling.
Connections, insulation and protection must work reliably when part of a conductor stops superconducting.
Complete systems must demonstrate competitive lifetime costs and reliability, including cooling, maintenance and replacement.

milestones.label: A utility circuit beats conventional cost and outage performance
milestones.explanation: A circuit several kilometers long would have to carry hundreds of megawatts in utility service with lower lifetime cost and fewer forced outages than a comparable conventional circuit. This would establish a practical transmission advantage.

milestones.label: A commercial generator becomes smaller or wastes less energy
milestones.explanation: A commercial generator would have to be smaller or waste less energy than a comparable copper-wound machine while maintaining acceptable total cost and reliability. This would establish a complete-machine benefit.

milestones.label: Material and system performance repeat independently
milestones.explanation: Material performance would have to repeat across independently made batches and useful lengths, with system results reproduced in independently assessable installations. This would establish dependable performance beyond isolated successes.

milestones.label: Tests establish service limits and maintenance needs
milestones.explanation: Demonstrations would have to define temperature, pressure, magnetic field, current, length, electrical duty, exposure and maintenance limits. This would establish where the equipment can reliably serve.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether a room-temperature material can combine useful current capacity, stability and scalable manufacture.
The mechanisms and lasting stability of the pressure-treated superconducting state remain open questions.
The service tests still need agreed observation periods and application-specific thresholds for acceptable cost and reliability.

page.title: Superconducting power cables and wind generators
page.definition: Utility cables and wind-generator coils use superconductors—materials with zero direct-current electrical resistance—while complete systems meet their service duties at lower life-cycle cost than conventional alternatives, including refrigeration. The generator coils create the rotor’s magnetic field.

goal.need: Cable comparisons must include refrigeration: in the roadmap’s 23 kV example, the refrigerator and auxiliaries consume more power than the superconducting conductor. EcoSwing targeted 40% lower generator mass and, assuming series production, 40% lower generator cost than commercial permanent-magnet direct-drive generators.

completion.title: A qualified superconducting power system enters commercial service with lower life-cycle cost.
completion.criterion: A completed and qualified superconducting cable or wind generator operates in commercial service and has lower whole-system life-cycle cost than a conventional alternative meeting the same power, duty and utility reliability requirements. Include installation, refrigeration, auxiliary electricity, maintenance and replacement over the utility’s evaluation period, using its discount rate. Apply separately to each device class. Shingal supplies reported cable-case evidence through commercial service and a net-present-value comparison; wind-generator completion remains unestablished in the cited results.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback criterion, synthesising the cited programmes’ system-level economic objectives.
completion.basis: Searches of DOE HTS programme goals, IEC 63075, the IEA HTS programme, the cable roadmap, SuperLink and EcoSwing found no shared numerical cost or reliability acceptance test. The fallback uses their whole-system economic objective. Shingal’s reported economic advantage is based on a net-present-value comparison. IEC 63075 qualifies AC cables and accessories but excludes the cooling system.

milestones.title: A superconducting cable or wind-generator technology is validated in the laboratory at TRL 4.
milestones.criterion: The cable or wind-generator technology is validated in laboratory tests, satisfying technology readiness level 4. In the EcoSwing work published on 25 October 2019, one full-scale rotor-coil design showed no thermal drift during tests at 30 K and 35 K, at currents up to about 120% of its expected operating current for at least 2 hours. This establishes component-level laboratory evidence before whole-generator demonstration.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G, TRL 4; a generic maturity criterion applied separately to each device class. EcoSwing explicitly used this TRL framework.

milestones.title: A superconducting cable or wind-generator technology is demonstrated in a relevant environment at TRL 6.
milestones.criterion: The cable or wind-generator technology is demonstrated in an environment relevant to its intended use, satisfying TRL 6. EcoSwing’s assembled rotor contained 40 coils; ground testing at Fraunhofer IWES reached coil temperatures of approximately 20–22 K after 14 days of cooling. A coil damaged during a quench was replaced before field installation. The project described its overall advance as TRL 4–5 to TRL 6–7.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G, TRL 6; a generic maturity criterion applied separately to each device class.

milestones.title: A superconducting cable or wind-generator prototype operates in its intended environment at TRL 7.
milestones.criterion: A system prototype is demonstrated in an operational environment, satisfying TRL 7. A 2026 paper reports that one 150 m SuperLink cable system, rated 110 kV and 500 MVA, operated for 6 months in Munich. One EcoSwing generator in a 3.6 MW turbine in Thyborøn supplied grid power for over 650 hours, reported on 25 October 2019. The generator paper assigns its superconducting coils TRL 7.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G, TRL 7; a generic maturity criterion applied separately to each device class.
milestones.threshold_quote: system prototype demonstration in operational environment

milestones.title: A complete superconducting cable or wind-generator system is qualified at TRL 8.
milestones.criterion: A complete system is qualified for its intended application, satisfying TRL 8. The cable roadmap classifies AC superconducting cables at TRL 8 and records commercial operation of one 1,056 m, 23 kV, 50 MVA Shingal cable system beginning in 2019. For wind generators, EcoSwing’s final consortium report records DNV-GL approval for prototype installation; commercial product qualification is not established by that approval. The consortium report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G, TRL 8; a generic maturity criterion applied separately to each device class. The cable roadmap explicitly uses TRL 8 for AC cables.

not_found: No source establishing commercial qualification together with a matched whole-system life-cycle cost comparison for a superconducting wind generator was found.
The full IEC 63075 technical test clauses could not be inspected; its catalogue and preview were accessible.
No primary confirmation of a commissioned 15 km SuperLink circuit or a binding commercial contract after 15 April 2026 was found.
